heading: Ohio is where the math still works.
lede: Coastal and Sun Belt multifamily traded on cap rate compression. The Midwest trades on operations. We would rather earn a return by running a building well than by hoping the exit cap is kinder than the entry.

points.title: Entry pricing that survives a bad year
points.body: Ohio multifamily still transacts well below replacement cost. A 1968 garden-style asset bought at $72,000 per unit cannot be rebuilt for three times that figure. That gap is the downside protection, and it does not depend on anyone’s forecast.

points.title: Spread, not compression
points.body: The current offering underwrites a 9.73% stabilized yield on cost against a 7.00% exit cap — roughly 270 basis points of spread. At a 7.75% exit and 2.0% rent growth, the projected LP IRR is still 11.7%. The return does not require the market to help.

points.title: Value-add only works if you can build
points.body: Most sponsors bid a renovation budget and hope a general contractor honors it; cost overruns land on the investor. Our construction company is in-house, so scope, schedule and trade pricing are controlled rather than quoted.

points.title: A market of private sellers
points.body: The 20-to-100-unit tier is owned largely by individuals and small partnerships rather than institutions. That is where direct relationships beat a broker’s bid list — and it is a deeper, less rate-sensitive buyer pool at exit, including 1031 exchange capital.
